stories.author: jasondavies
stories.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
stories.groq_label: Alessandro Masullo's draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is being released urgently for community review.
stories.groq_explain: The post is a brief, urgent notice posted on November 20, 2026 by a member of the American Mathematical Society’s Executive Committee and Board of Trustees. The author says they are currently at an AMS meeting but needed to share a draft of a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Masullo. According to the announcement, the proof has been examined for months by Brian Conrad, who has provided extensive feedback that is being incorporated, and the reviewers consider it promising. The author notes that the work is entirely human‑produced, with no AI involvement, and that the plan was originally to bring Masullo to Stanford for a year to polish the manuscript before a formal announcement. Because of the perceived importance, the author wants to release the current draft now so that the mathematical community can review it, formalize any details, and fill any small gaps that may appear. The post emphasizes confidence in Conrad’s judgment and expresses hope that the proof will ultimately be correct. No actual mathematical content or the draft itself is included in the page; only a generic WordPress footer appears after the announcement. The message matters because a valid proof of GRH would resolve one of the most significant open problems in analytic number theory, with far‑reaching consequences throughout mathematics.

stories.author: QueensGambit
stories.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
stories.groq_label: Architects must push back on requirements that harm performance and choose logging approaches that balance speed, security, and data needs.
stories.groq_explain:
The article recounts a recent incident in which a colleague added extensive logging to a Google Forms add‑on in order to monitor new installations. By trying to capture the user’s email, then the user ID, and finally falling back to an error message, the code made several API calls on every install. Because the logging ran before the welcome screen, the screen took about fifteen seconds to load, creating a serious performance problem.

The author explains that a senior developer or architect would have approached the requirement differently. Instead of attempting to fetch personal data synchronously, they would have logged only a timestamp, informing the marketing team that follow‑up email addresses could not be obtained at install time. If the marketing team needed the email, the architect would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or ID asynchronously, while ensuring that any server calls respected security constraints and did not require unauthenticated payloads.

The piece then critiques AI code generators, noting that while they can produce functional code, they lack awareness of scale, user volume, and the trade‑offs between performance and security. AI tends to follow the literal requirements without pushing back, which can lead to slow, insecure, or overly complex implementations. The author argues that the correct approach is to specify architectural constraints first, design the data model, and then let AI generate code within those limits. Whenever a requirement would change the architecture, the tool should ask for confirmation rather than silently rewriting it.

A broader point is made about the changing role of developers. Many developers who excel at coding are being moved into architect positions without clear guidance. Their new responsibilities include challenging unrealistic requirements, designing data models, constraining AI‑generated code, and reviewing implementations for performance and maintainability. The author stresses that while the hands‑on coding work may be increasingly automated, the need for architectural oversight remains, and developers should adapt by learning to think like architects. The article serves as a warning and a call to action for developers who have been “promoted” to architects without being told.

stories.author: ankitvgupta
stories.title: Vibecoding an Inference Chip
stories.groq_label: A large language model was successfully deployed on an FPGA using AI coding agents, reaching real‑time inference speeds.
stories.groq_explain:
The author recounts how they used AI coding agents to program an FPGA to run a large‑language‑model inference engine, a process they refer to as “vibe‑coding.” Starting with only a basic understanding of field‑programmable gate arrays—reconfigurable chips that can be programmed at the hardware level for potential performance gains—they set out to see whether modern large language models could handle the low‑level C++ and Verilog work required for such a task.  

Using AWS F2 instances that provide FPGA hardware with 16 GB of high‑bandwidth memory, the author asked Codex to reserve an instance and began an extended experiment that combined automated agent work with occasional human prompts. The goal was to run a ternary‑weight model, a design from DeepGrove that is suited to memory‑limited environments and already performs well on macOS.  

Over several days the AI agents, running under the Conductor orchestration framework, generated roughly three million lines of code and parsed thirty million lines of output. They iteratively refined the design, moving from a baseline implementation to a version that achieved a thirty‑three‑fold speed increase, reaching 213 tokens per second compared with the initial performance. Key optimizations included a head loader that accessed both memory banks simultaneously, a prefetch policy, timing fixes, and a modest reduction in clock frequency to avoid random faults.  

The author emphasizes that most prompts to the agents were simple, such as urging the model to be more creative or to aim for a two‑fold speedup, with occasional domain‑specific suggestions like speculative decoding or porting CPU‑bound code to the FPGA. Both the Astra and Opus agents performed adequately, and the human contribution—particularly a prompt supplied by the DeepGrove founders—provided the most useful guidance, steering the agents away from overly time‑consuming tasks like cycle‑accurate simulation.  

The experiment cost about ten thousand dollars in Claude and OpenAI token usage, demonstrating that large token budgets can enable extensive autoresearch loops without prohibitive expense. The author notes that even without deep personal experience in C++ or Verilog, the AI‑driven workflow made the project feasible, highlighting a new paradigm where developers can leverage powerful language models to explore hardware programming domains that were previously considered too labor‑intensive. This work suggests that with sufficient prompting and compute resources, AI agents can effectively bridge the gap between high‑level model design and low‑level hardware implementation, potentially accelerating the adoption of custom inference accelerators.

stories.author: archon1410
stories.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_label: AI assisted Lean formalizations claim proofs of finite time blowup for three dimensional Euler and Navier Stokes equations and a Lean only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_explain: The post announces three major developments that have been produced with extensive AI assistance and formalized in the Lean proof assistant. First, Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu have created a human‑readable proof that the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions can develop a finite‑time singularity. The proof is also available as a formal Lean verification. Second, Alpöge and Buckmaster, again using heavy AI support, have generated a proof of finite‑time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in three dimensions. This paper is technically readable and follows a known strategy: constructing an approximate discretely self‑similar solution numerically and then applying rigorous perturbation theory to turn it into an exact solution. Although the overall argument is clear, a fully polished, professionally written version is still pending. Third, Alpöge has produced an enormous Lean‑only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The proof appears to rely on deep recent advances in the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry. Verification of this proof is ongoing in a dedicated Lean Zulip thread, where discussion is now limited to the Lean‑related aspects. The author notes that these results will soon be reported in other outlets and references a Mastodon post by Buckmaster that discusses the first two results. The announcements are significant because they claim breakthroughs on two of the most famous open problems in analysis—the Euler and Navier–Stokes blowup questions—and on a central conjecture in number theory, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, while also highlighting the emerging role of AI and formal proof assistants in producing and checking complex mathematics.

stories.author: khalidkhair
stories.title: Running two PSP emulators on one Switch 2 and sharing one via GameShare
stories.groq_label: An experimental PPSSPP build runs two isolated emulator instances on a Switch 2 to stream one to another device via GameShare.
stories.groq_explain:
This document details an experimental branch of the PPSSPP emulator, known as ppsspp-nx2, designed for the Nintendo Switch 2. The project experiments with running a second, independent PPSSPP guest emulator on a host Switch 2 console and streaming its display and controls to a second console using the system GameShare feature. Rather than simply mirroring controls or acting as a secondary controller, the setup runs two distinct emulator instances simultaneously inside a single application process on the host console.

Building and installing the experimental software requires specific build scripts and deployment commands with experimental flags enabled. It installs as a separate application alongside the standard single-instance PPSSPP installation, leaving existing host settings, saves, and application files untouched. Launching requires a GameShare-capable native title override, as generic title overrides do not grant the necessary system context for GameShare. To start sharing, the user selects the GameShare option from the host application menu, and the client console joins through its system GameShare screen, allowing both consoles to browse game files stored on the host console SD card.

Underneath the hood, the project links a second PPSSPP core into a relocatable object, renaming all defined core global symbols to ensure strict isolation between the host and guest cores. Both instances possess independent settings, memory stick directories, JIT registries, and Vulkan rendering contexts while sharing the same underlying OS process. The host runs at 1080p resolution at 120 hertz, whereas the guest renders offscreen at 720p targeted at 60 frames per second. Completed guest frames are read back by the CPU and delivered to a separate display layer for streaming. This readback step introduces CPU overhead, meaning zero-copy rendering is not implemented.

Storage, audio, and controller inputs are isolated between the host and guest instances. Guest inputs do not interact with the host emulator, and guest audio is directed to a dedicated per-guest queue, which has been verified to play audio on the client console. Native text-entry applets for the guest are currently disabled due to missing remote routing capabilities. For local PSP ad hoc multiplayer, the application runs a local packet relay and discovery service on loopback ports on the host console. Because both emulator instances physically run on the host Switch 2, multiplayer traffic remains entirely internal without needing external network relays, Wi-Fi IP configuration, or UPnP setup.

This experiment is significant because it explores multi-instance emulation and single-console hosting of remote multiplayer gaming using native Switch 2 hardware features. However, current tests serve as a preliminary technical checkpoint, and compilation and host tests do not yet establish console operation or acceptable performance when actively running two games at the same time.

stories.author: lwhsiao
stories.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
stories.groq_label: A 27B language model autonomously rewrites its own weights through reasoning and forward passes, achieving higher accuracy without gradients or external training
stories.groq_explain:
The paper “Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights” presents a novel approach in which a language model modifies its own parameters without any gradient‑based training. The authors demonstrate that a frozen 27‑billion‑parameter model can evaluate its own outputs, identify failures, and rewrite its weight matrices through forward‑only computation. This self‑rewriting process, described as the model acting as its own optimizer, yields measurable improvements: the edited model becomes 6.6 percentage points more accurate on unseen problems compared with its original version. 

The method proceeds iteratively. After each edit, the model tests the modification on practice problems and only retains changes that demonstrably improve performance. Over eight consecutive editing sessions the model’s accuracy continues to rise. The authors also show that a severely damaged copy of the model, which initially solves almost no tasks, can be repaired through self‑rewriting to recover more than eighty percent of the original accuracy on image‑based tasks it has never encountered. 

Experiments across a family of models reveal that this capability emerges only at larger scales; smaller models either make no edits or degrade performance, whereas the largest model both improves and repairs itself. Unlike traditional test‑time scaling, the gains from self‑rewriting are written directly into the weights, incurring no additional cost per inference. Unlike conventional training, the process requires only forward passes, matching the computational profile of serving. 

The authors argue that the separation between training and inference is a limitation of current tools rather than an inherent property of intelligence. Self‑rewriting is positioned as a necessary step toward recursive self‑improvement, enabling a model to continuously upgrade itself throughout its lifetime without larger successors, external harnesses, prompt engineering, or additional training phases. This work suggests a path toward more autonomous and lifelong learning systems in artificial intelligence.

stories.author: unchar1
stories.title: I'll never buy Framework hardware again
stories.groq_label: Framework's defective laptop and unhelpful support led to a decision to stop buying their hardware.
stories.groq_explain:
The author, a consultant who runs a small business called aljuna.tech, describes a very negative experience with a Framework Laptop 16 that his company purchased for a developer. The laptop cost about three thousand euros and arrived with a hardware fault that prevented it from booting properly. The keyboard was not detected, causing the touchpad and other input modules to be non‑functional, and the BIOS showed a “missing input module” error before any operating system was installed.

The support process turned into a prolonged, repetitive series of troubleshooting steps that the author characterises as a scripted “loop”. Over the course of several weeks, Framework support repeatedly asked for the same information—photos of the mid‑plate and keyboard, verification of the shipping address, BIOS resets, driver reinstallations—even though the author had already supplied these details. Different agents handled each email and seemed unaware of the previous messages.

The developer eventually used Framework’s own diagnostic tool, framework_tool, to isolate the problem. The tool revealed that the keyboard module was being identified as a numpad, causing the system to see two numpads and no keyboard, which in turn kept the power rail for input modules disabled. This indicated that the keyboard itself was defective, not the mid‑plate as Framework later claimed.

In early September Framework sent a replacement mid‑plate, but the issue persisted because the faulty keyboard remained. After further insistence, Framework finally agreed to replace the keyboard in October. The new keyboard worked for normal typing, but introduced a new bug where pressing the “c” key generated an extra delete escape sequence, a problem not seen with an external keyboard.

The author concludes that the hardware itself was not the primary issue; rather, the support experience was unprofessional, inefficient, and dismissive. He has decided to ban any future Framework purchases at his company and warns others to avoid the brand. The story matters because it highlights the risks of relying on a company’s customer service for high‑end, modular hardware, especially when the product is marketed as repairable and Linux‑friendly. It also serves as a cautionary tale for organizations considering large investments in niche laptops that may not have robust support infrastructure.

stories.author: trotro
stories.title: Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
stories.groq_label: Repository provides the Navier‑Stokes finite‑time blow‑up paper and its accompanying Lean 4 formalization.
stories.groq_explain:
The repository hosts the research paper titled “Finite‑time blow‑up for the Navier–Stokes equations” by L. Alpöge and T. Buckmaster, together with a Lean 4 formalization that accompanies the results. The paper itself is a 79‑page document dated 20 November 2026 and is provided as a PDF in the directory paper/. The Lean component is a complete Lean 4 package (compatible with Lean v4.33.1 and Mathlib) placed under the directory lean/. 

Within the Lean folder the README.md explains how the formal statements correspond to the main theorems of the paper—specifically Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2 and the material in Appendix B—and notes where the formal proofs differ from those in the manuscript. The NOTICE file describes the content of each statement file and what has been proved. The top‑level statement files define the concepts and state the theorems, initially containing “sorry” placeholders. The file Solution.lean supplies the actual proofs drawn from the library in lean/Breakdown/. For each theorem a comparator JSON file links the statement file with Solution.lean, lists the theorems that must match, and restricts the allowed axioms to propext, Quot.sound and Classical.choice. Building the package from the lean/ directory requires running the command “lake exe cache get” followed by “lake build”. Because the library is large—about 2,270 files and 600 000 lines—a full build demands considerable memory and time. 

The repository does not contain any numerical data, nor the cryptographic certificate whose hash is referenced in the paper; the authors state that the certificate will be released separately. The rigorous computational verification of the certificate, which uses interval arithmetic at 128‑bit precision via the Arb library through FLINT, is also absent from the repository. Likewise, the source files for the paper itself are not included. 

The Lean text reflects the working repository used for the paper, with a single patch applied on 20 November 2026. This patch modifies certain cell‑layer statements and dependent library proofs: a bound’s weight changes from \(m^{2}+\tfrac14\) to \((|m|+\tfrac12)^{2}\), one cell constant may be zero, and the set of model harmonics in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper presents the conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when the repository was assembled. 

Overall, the repository provides both the mathematical manuscript and a substantial formal verification effort, linking analytic results on finite‑time blow‑up for the Navier–Stokes equations with machine‑checked proofs, while indicating which components remain external to the code base.

stories.author: shioyama
stories.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
stories.groq_label: AI systems autonomously designed and verified a new CPU architecture called Frostbite that achieves a major increase in performance per watt over traditional CPU cores.
stories.groq_explain:
Frostbite is a general-purpose CPU architecture and instruction set designed, implemented, and verified entirely by artificial intelligence systems. Created to overcome decades of stagnation in CPU core performance improvements, Frostbite achieved a 4.59x increase in performance per watt compared to a modern, silicon-proven dual-issue in-order superscalar CPU core, while also delivering a step-function gain in performance per area.

The architecture departs from traditional hardware designs by utilizing interaction nets, a model where programs are represented as graphs of nodes. In this model, every step is local, dependencies are explicit, and every value has exactly one owner. By eliminating shared mutable state, Frostbite removes the need for complex out-of-order execution machinery, conventional threading, locks, deep cache hierarchies, and expensive cache coherence protocols. Instead, computation occurs through local graph rewrites, and data is stored in small local memories directly adjacent to where it is used.

The AI systems created Frostbite with zero architectural priors, utilizing agent swarms to iterate across the entire development stack, including the compiler, instruction set architecture, microarchitecture, register-transfer level code, verification, and final physical layout files. The architecture was evaluated across 25 workloads divided into search sets and held-out evaluation sets, covering algorithms such as fast Fourier transforms, radix sorting, matrix decomposition, Kalman filters, principal component analysis, finite element analysis, and data decompression.

This work matters because it proves that AI systems can co-design hardware and software to discover radically performant architectural primitives that human designers might miss. The success of Frostbite suggests that future computing hardware, including datacenter CPUs, AI accelerators, networking switches, and network interface cards, will likely undergo similar AI-driven architectural transformations.

stories.author: sammatilda
stories.title: If you can't explain something in simple terms, you don't understand it (2017)
stories.groq_label: The ability to explain complex concepts in simple terms serves as the ultimate proof of true understanding.
stories.groq_explain:
This article explores the concept that true mastery of a complex topic requires the ability to explain it in simple terms. It highlights the teaching philosophy of Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman, as well as modern corporate standards at Apple, to demonstrate how simplifying difficult concepts serves as a test of genuine understanding.

In the early 1960s, Feynman delivered a series of physics lectures at Caltech. Colleague David Goodstein once asked Feynman to explain a complex concept, specifically why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics, in simple terms. Feynman attempted to prepare an introductory freshman lecture on the subject, but returned days later stating he could not reduce it to that level, concluding that the inability to simplify it meant scientists did not truly understand it. Feynman was well known for producing accessible explanations of everyday physics, such as how fire is stored sunshine, how rubber bands function, how trains turn on tracks, and how magnets work. At the same time, he was quick to admit when he or the scientific community lacked deep comprehension. For instance, he openly acknowledged his inability to explain magnetic force using familiar concepts, and he famously remarked that nobody understands quantum mechanics, despite having won a Nobel Prize for his work on the subject. A note found on his blackboard at the time of his death in 1988 read that what he could not create, he did not understand.

The principle of using simple explanations to demonstrate complete comprehension also applies outside of physics. John Gruber notes that engineers at Apple are expected to explain complex technologies in clear, easily understood terms. This requirement is not just so executives can understand the technology, but serves as direct proof that the engineer understands the product completely. 

The main point of the text is that simplicity in communication is the ultimate benchmark of knowledge. Being unable to explain a concept simply, or needing to rely on overly dense language, reveals gaps in understanding rather than expertise.

stories.author: dotcoma
stories.title: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
stories.groq_label: Signal is blocking screen captures on mobile operating systems to prevent integrated AI agents from accessing and storing private user data.
stories.groq_explain:
Signal published an article explaining how recent artificial intelligence integrations in major mobile and desktop operating systems threaten user privacy. As Google, Apple, and Microsoft deeply integrate agentic AI features like Google Gemini Intelligence, Apple Siri AI Onscreen Awareness, and Microsoft Recall into Android, iOS, and Windows, these AI systems operate by scanning screen content. This scanning process captures sensitive Signal message data and makes it accessible to local databases or remote servers outside of Signal control, which fundamentally undermines the application's ability to independently guarantee message privacy.

To counter this threat, Signal is extending its screenshot blocking protections to iOS and Android to restrict operating system AI assistants from reading screen data, expanding on measures previously implemented for Windows 11. Users have the option to disable screenshot blocking in Signal settings, though doing so risks exposing their conversation data to AI systems. Signal acknowledges that screenshot blocking is an incomplete defense because AI agents can still potentially access application data through other avenues, such as reading the device filesystem or misusing deep system accessibility permissions, as seen with third-party agents like Meta Muse.

Signal highlights major challenges in protecting user data, including a lack of clear documentation from operating system providers, which forced Signal developers to conduct forensic investigations to figure out how AI agents access data. Furthermore, operating system companies currently do not provide simple tools for developers to opt out of AI data scraping without making severe compromises to the core app experience, which has prevented Signal from implementing similar protections on macOS. 

Signal is calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to address these privacy concerns by providing clear documentation on how their AI agents function and creating simple, well-documented technical tools that allow application developers to opt out of AI data access and processing across screens, filesystems, notifications, and APIs. This issue matters because millions of users rely on Signal for secure communication, and operating-system-level AI data collection poses an existential threat to application-level privacy guarantees.

stories.author: qtqtqt
stories.title: GIMP now has UI tests
stories.groq_label: GIMP implements automated UI tests to detect interface regressions early.
stories.groq_explain:
The announcement explains that GIMP now includes an automated graphical user interface (UI) testing platform. Because GIMP’s menus, dialogs and tools are tightly interlinked, changes to one part of the interface can unintentionally break another, and such problems may only be noticed after a user reports them. The new UI tests run each time contributor changes are merged, allowing developers to catch interface regressions early.

The article distinguishes UI tests from existing unit tests. Unit tests verify isolated pieces of code, such as the handling of XCF files, but they do not open a real window and therefore cannot confirm that dialogs appear or that menu actions work. Earlier GUI tests interacted directly with core code or simulated input events, yet they could not exercise the complete interface and were fragile. UI tests, by contrast, launch a full instance of GIMP, perform real user actions like clicking menus and buttons, and then examine the resulting state. If the outcome is incorrect the test fails and reports the problem.

At the time of writing, thirteen tests are in place. They verify that GIMP starts and shows its main window, that the Welcome dialog behaves correctly, that creating a new image, exporting a PNG, swapping colors, editing foreground colors, adding and deleting layers, undo and redo, zooming, selecting tools, using the bucket‑fill tool, saving preferences, and flattening an image all function as expected.

The tests are designed to run without a physical display. Each test creates a small hidden desktop environment, runs GIMP inside it, and then tears the environment down. To locate UI elements the tests rely on the accessibility data GIMP provides for screen readers, which also improves GIMP’s accessibility. The testing framework uses dogtail, a Python tool for UI automation. Because dogtail originally required a screen, the GIMP developers added a new feature to dogtail that enables headless operation; this contribution has been merged upstream so other projects can benefit. Currently the tests run only on Linux (both X11 and Wayland) because dogtail does not yet support Windows or macOS.

The article credits Harsh Verma for writing the UI tests and the dogtail enhancement, Jehan and Michal Odehnal for reviewing them, and points to the full merge request for more detail. It invites community involvement, noting that GIMP has many more dialogs and tools that could be covered. Developers are encouraged to write additional tests following the guide on the GIMP developer site, which explains how to create new tests and diagnose failures.

Overall, the introduction of UI tests represents a significant step toward more reliable releases, earlier bug detection, and better accessibility for GIMP users.

The piece likely details how the command works, the performance improvements over previous approaches, and the steps needed to use it in production. stories.author: JacobHenner
stories.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)
stories.groq_label: Fixes CVE‑2026‑121481 buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock, adds input validation to EVP_DecodeBlock and corrects base64encode length check.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes a pull request to the OpenSSL project that addresses a critical security flaw identified as CVE‑2026‑121481. The vulnerability is a buffer overflow in the function EVP_EncodeBlock, which can be triggered by invalid inputs and lead to undefined behavior or potential exploitation. The proposed changes resolve the overflow by returning ‑1 for invalid inputs and, in a later revision, by invoking OPENSSL_assert when such inputs are detected. The same defensive logic is applied to the related function EVP_DecodeBlock.

In addition to fixing the encoding and decoding functions, the patch corrects an incorrect length check in the base64encode routine found in http_client.c. The updates also include revisions to the documentation to reflect the new behavior, especially for zero‑length inputs, and new test cases that verify the fixes.

The discussion around the pull request shows a review timeline: an initial approval by a contributor named nhorman on November 11 2026, requests for changes on November 12 2026, a hold placed by bob‑beck for community consensus, and subsequent commits that refine the fix. Additional context mentions a related fuzzer commit and performance testing of the AVX2 encoder versus a scalar implementation, as well as versioning details for OpenSSL 4.1.0.

The significance of this change lies in preventing a high‑severity (CVSS 9.8) vulnerability that could allow attackers to cause memory corruption, crashes, or arbitrary code execution when OpenSSL processes malformed base64 data. By adding proper input validation, assertions, and documentation, the patch improves the security and robustness of OpenSSL’s base64 handling functions. The pull request has been merged, indicating that the fix is now part of the OpenSSL codebase.

stories.author: emot
stories.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
stories.groq_label: Vint Cerf says TCP/IP remains unpatented because it was deliberately kept open to ensure universal access and collaboration
stories.groq_explain:
The article announces the launch of a new technology and science podcast called Future Stories, whose first episode features an interview with Vint Cerf, the co‑designer of TCP/IP. The conversation, recorded over Zoom on October 14, runs about fifty‑six minutes and is available as a full audio file, a transcript, and short clips. Cerf, now 83, recently left Google after more than two decades and is helping to start a company called Tolero, which aims to build software for an interplanetary Internet, noting that “the speed of light is too slow.” He reflects on the open nature of the Internet, saying that because future allies cannot be predicted, the network must remain accessible to everyone.

During the interview Cerf shares several anecdotes that illustrate the collaborative spirit behind early networking work. He recounts a two‑week debugging effort that was solved in thirty seconds when his friend Steve Crocker identified the problem, emphasizing the value of teamwork. He also tells the story of how a commercial network in San Diego was named CERFnet after a naming conflict with a Dutch network; Cerf approved the use of his name despite initial hesitation and celebrated the launch by smashing a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router. Another episode describes his attempt to link France’s Minitel service to MCI Mail, which ultimately failed, leaving him still puzzled.

The piece also mentions a humorous 1992 “IP on Everything” striptease photo Cerf posted in response to a question about his attire, and his concerns that future generations may be unable to interpret the digital records we leave behind. He shows a plaque from the original ARPANET Interface Message Processor, a large packet‑switching computer given to him when he left ARPA in 1982.

While AI is not a main focus of the interview, Cerf’s clear thinking on the topic is noted. The article provides links to the full conversation, the transcript, and a Portuguese write‑up, and invites listeners to subscribe, share, and suggest future guests. It also references a 2024 segment from Cerf’s earlier podcast that revisited the 1974 TCP paper by Cerf and Bob Kahn, explaining how TCP was later split into TCP and IP and became the core of the modern Internet launched by DARPA in 1983. The overall message underscores the importance of open, collaborative development in creating the enduring infrastructure of the Internet.

stories.author: hn-aarvin
stories.title: Gemini 4 Neon is the new #1 on the Models Engineering Index

stories.groq_explain:

The index combines raw performance scores with cost‑adjusted multipliers, producing a ranking that highlights both how well a model solves engineering problems and how efficiently it does so.

stories.author: cybermango
stories.title: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
stories.groq_label: Claude solved two longstanding black‑hole quantum‑gravity problems by completing a decades‑old phase‑transition calculation and finding the exact bound of a basic holographic test.
stories.groq_explain:
Claude, the Anthropic AI system, has resolved two long‑standing theoretical physics problems that involve black holes and the search for a quantum theory of gravity. The first problem concerned a phase transition that occurs when a theoretical universe is heated. At low temperature the universe contains a gas of particles, but above a certain temperature a black hole forms. Hawking and Page showed in 1983 that this transition is abrupt, but their calculation relied on general relativity, which breaks down when the universe becomes very small and spacetime loses a definite shape. In the quantum description of the same situation the transition was known to exist, yet it was unclear whether it was abrupt or smooth. In 2003 a group of physicists outlined the extremely complex calculation that would decide the question, but it was never completed. Claude assembled a small research group of copies of itself, solved nearly every component of the calculation independently, and cross‑checked the results against known limits. It demonstrated that the transition remains abrupt even in the regime where spacetime is fuzzy, indicating that the sudden formation of a black hole is a feature of the underlying quantum theory rather than an artifact of classical relativity.

The second problem involved a simplified model universe with two spatial dimensions. Physicists use a “bootstrap” approach to rule out inconsistent candidate theories of quantum gravity by establishing limits on the properties of black holes in that model. Since 2009 a numerical ceiling on the mass of the lightest black hole has been suggested, but a rigorous proof of the optimal ceiling has been missing, and the best proven bound fell short of the numerical evidence. Claude’s “Fable 5.2” identified a pattern in the numerical data that had been overlooked and applied a mathematical technique from another field to compute the exact ceiling for the simplest bootstrap method, proving that the bound cannot be lowered further. While this does not pinpoint the correct theory, it narrows the space of viable candidates.

Both findings do not describe our actual universe nor have immediate practical applications, but they advance the broader effort to reconcile quantum mechanics with general relativity. The article also explains that Claude’s work emerged from an experiment by Anthropic researcher Hongbin Chen, who asked the AI to list promising open problems in black‑hole physics. Claude produced a set of candidates, after which multiple AI agents worked in parallel, sharing progress and collaborating on related sub‑problems. The post links to the preprints where the detailed technical arguments are presented.

stories.author: D_R_Farrell
stories.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
stories.groq_label: Onlook is an open-source desktop tool that lets designers visually edit live codebases using AI agents.
stories.groq_explain: Onlook is an open‑source developer tool aimed at designers who want to create and edit real applications visually rather than through a terminal. It presents a live running version of a project on an infinite canvas, allowing designers to explore ideas side by side across mobile, tablet and desktop frames. The tool connects to existing AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, ChatGPT or Codex; users bring their own model credentials and the agent can edit the actual files in the project based on natural‑language prompts. Onlook works directly with any local Git repository: it launches the developer’s own dev server, displays the live app in the canvas, and tracks changes through Git. The application runs as a desktop, local‑first Electron app, so code never leaves the user’s machine and no cloud accounts or environment keys are required. Designers can export their work as self‑contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF for hand‑off, review or sharing, and they can also generate pull requests from within the interface. The product supports parallel projects as tabs, safe work‑tree copies that keep the original folder untouched, and can import GitHub repositories or start new codebases from scratch. Onlook’s technology stack includes Electron, React 19, Zustand, CodeMirror and various tooling such as Bun and Turborepo. The project is released under the Apache 2.0 license, encouraging forks and customizations, and it gathers optional usage analytics to improve the app. By allowing designers to work directly on real codebases with AI assistance and visual feedback, Onlook aims to bridge the gap between design and development, reducing the need for separate mockup rebuilding and streamlining the hand‑off process.

stories.author: Terretta
stories.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
stories.groq_label: UK court orders the government to acknowledge it issued a secret Technical Capability Notice requiring Apple to modify iCloud encryption.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains that the United Kingdom government has been compelled to admit that it issued Apple a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN) under Section 253 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. A TCN is a confidential order that can require a technology company to modify its services to enable government surveillance. The existence of such an order had been denied by the government, which maintained a “neither confirm nor deny” stance, even though the order had been reported in the press. 

The dispute began after a Washington Post investigation in February 2025 revealed that the UK had ordered Apple to provide back‑door access to encrypted iCloud data, affecting users worldwide. In response, Apple withdrew its Advanced Data Protection (ADP) feature – an optional add‑on that extends end‑to‑end encryption so that Apple itself cannot decrypt the data – from new UK customers. Apple also stated it would not build any back‑door or master key, but was prohibited from mentioning the TCN publicly. The initial order was later withdrawn after diplomatic pressure, but a second TCN, reportedly limited to British users, was issued, prompting Apple to launch a fresh legal challenge in 2026. 

Civil‑rights groups Liberty and Privacy International, represented by Ben Jaffey KC, challenged the government’s secrecy at a hearing of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal on 17 September. They argued that keeping the order secret was untenable because its existence was already public and that the secrecy policy was damaging to justice. The government countered that disclosure could harm national security by revealing which companies were subject to such orders. The tribunal rejected that argument, ruling that the government had not shown any national‑security harm from acknowledging the notice. The tribunal did not decide whether the order was lawful or what technical changes were required, but it forced the government to admit the notice’s existence.

The article also highlights the practical impact of the dispute on users. Because Apple stopped offering ADP to new UK customers in February 2025, existing users who had already enabled the feature retained it, while newer users could not. This created a “two‑tier” encryption system in which two people with identical iPhones and iCloud accounts – illustrated as fictional “Alice” (who enabled ADP) and “Bill” (who did not) – have different levels of protection. The author argues that this disparity undermines the expectation of uniform privacy for all users and raises broader concerns about government attempts to compel companies to weaken their own security measures. The significance of the tribunal’s decision lies in breaking the government’s secrecy shield, setting a precedent for greater transparency about surveillance orders, and exposing the tension between national‑security objectives and individual privacy rights.

stories.author: datascientist
stories.title: Pete warden on local AI, open models, voice interfaces, the future of hardware
stories.groq_label: Local AI is becoming more capable and economically viable, driving a shift from cloud to on-device models and new hardware.
stories.groq_explain:
The page presents a podcast episode titled “Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware.” In the interview, Ben Lorica talks with Pete Warden, a veteran deep‑learning engineer and co‑creator of the Moonshine Voice project, about why artificial intelligence is increasingly being run on devices rather than in cloud services. Warden explains that local AI has become far more capable than most people realize, noting that open‑weight models can now be quantized and run on laptops, browsers, and even small edge devices without a large loss of performance. He points out that the main obstacle to wider adoption is not technical but economic: cloud providers can monetize SaaS APIs, whereas locally running models give no direct revenue stream, so large companies have little incentive to market them.

The conversation covers several key themes. First, the rapid progress of open models means they are only a few months behind commercial offerings from firms such as Anthropic and OpenAI, and they are already competitive on benchmarks. Second, running AI locally can improve privacy, reduce latency, and enable voice as a more natural computing interface that goes beyond current assistants like Siri and Alexa. Warden emphasizes that low‑latency speech models are crucial for a good user experience, and that designing voice interfaces must account for failure and human feedback.

The interview also contrasts specialized speech models with end‑to‑end or multimodal approaches, arguing that specialized models can be more efficient for voice tasks. Warden discusses the economics of local AI, suggesting that as tools become easier to use—citing examples like Ollama—developers will find it viable to embed models directly into operating systems and applications. He highlights emerging hardware trends that could shift the AI landscape away from GPU‑centric inference, including high‑bandwidth flash storage and new processor designs from companies such as Apple and NVIDIA that are optimized for on‑device inference.

Overall, the episode argues that local AI is poised to become a mainstream alternative to cloud‑based services, driven by advances in open models, quantization techniques, and hardware. This shift matters because it promises greater user privacy, lower latency, and new business models that give enterprises more control over their AI workloads. The page includes a full transcript of the conversation, links to the video version, and references to related topics such as TinyML, sensor‑driven AI, and the broader debate over frontier AI regulation.

stories.author: krthr
stories.title: Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
stories.groq_label: Fanzines.app lets users design and export correctly ordered 8‑page A4 foldable zines directly in the browser.
stories.groq_explain:
The article explains how to create an eight‑page foldable zine from a single A4 sheet and introduces a web tool called fanzines.app that simplifies the layout process. The author describes the traditional manual method: fold the A4 paper in half three times, cut along the center crease, and fold into a cross to produce a booklet without staples or glue, then fill it with photos, poems or notes. The difficulty with the conventional approach lies in arranging the flat sheet on a computer, because the pages must be placed in a non‑intuitive order and the top row needs to be printed upside down. To eliminate the need for rotating images and manually checking column order in graphics software, the author built fanzines.app, which lets users design each page right‑side up in the browser and automatically generates a 300 DPI PDF with the correct rotation and layout. All processing remains local, so no images are uploaded to a server.

Recent updates to the editor address several usability issues. The sidebar now groups page thumbnails into actual spreads that reflect how the physical booklet folds, and a new Spread view shows the facing page at lower opacity for easier alignment. Drag‑and‑drop support lets users import a folder of eight photos, with the interface indicating which pages will receive each image in reading order. The inspector has been streamlined: Fill, Fit and Center buttons replace manual coordinate entry, while precise numeric fields are still available in a collapsible section using millimetres for layout dimensions and points for text. Before exporting, a Review screen displays the full unfolded A4 sheet with optional cut and fold line overlays and a 5 mm safe margin that scales the layout to about 95 % to accommodate typical printer edge clipping. Additional enhancements include a mobile‑friendly interface that shows one page at a time with a bottom thumbnail strip, and bilingual support for English and Spanish, with language changes preserving the current work.

The article matters because it offers a practical, privacy‑preserving solution for anyone who wants to make small, self‑published booklets without the hassle of manual page ordering, making the creative process faster and more accessible on both desktop and mobile devices.
